Why does this style rule that out, and what is it actually requiring of the data underneath?
reference: The two are the same constraint seen from opposite ends. Cursor pagination requires a unique, unchanging ordering over the result set — typically a creation timestamp — and it encodes the client's position as an opaque cursor relative to that ordering rather than as an index. That requirement is what buys you the consistent view you switched for: the client never sees the same item twice even while other clients insert rows mid-scroll. It is also exactly why page numbers are gone — a cursor names a position in an ordering, so the scheme deliberately does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. The ordering field needs to be unchanging and unique-or-nearly-unique (millisecond timestamps are the canonical example) and must not be a float, since precision errors give wrong results. You set it via the pagination class's `ordering` attribute, and if you combine it with OrderingFilter you should strongly consider restricting which fields clients may order by. Deep links have to be re-expressed as saved cursors, not page indices.

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly CursorPagination ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set.

You can modify the ordering by overriding the 'ordering' attribute on the pagination class, or by using the OrderingFilter filter class together with CursorPagination. When used with OrderingFilter you should strongly consider restricting the fields that the user may order by.
Should not be a float. Precision errors easily lead to incorrect results.

Cursor pagination rules out deep-linking to specific pages because it does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions in the result set. It only provides forward and reverse controls [1].

Regarding the data underneath, this style requires a unique, unchanging ordering of items to paginate against [1]. Specifically, the ordering field must satisfy the following requirements:
*   **Unchanging:** It must be a value set only once, such as a timestamp or slug [2].
*   **Unique or nearly unique:** While it should ideally be unique (e.g., millisecond precision timestamps), the implementation supports non-strictly-unique values by using "position plus offset" logic [2, 7].
*   **Non-nullable:** It must be a non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string [2].
*   **Data type:** It should not be a float to avoid precision errors [2].
*   **Indexing:** The field must have a database index [2].

### CursorPagination¶ {#cursorpagination}

The cursor-based pagination presents an opaque "cursor" indicator that the client may use to page through the result set. This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.

Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Cursor based pagination is more complex than other schemes. It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. However it does provide the following benefits:

Proper usage of cursor pagination should have an ordering field that satisfies the following:

Should be an unchanging value, such as a timestamp, slug, or other field that is only set once, on creation.
Should be unique, or nearly unique. Millisecond precision timestamps are a good example. This implementation of cursor pagination uses a smart "position plus offset" style that allows it to properly support not-strictly-unique values as the ordering.
Should be a non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string.
Should not be a float. Precision errors easily lead to incorrect results.
Hint: use decimals instead.
(If you already have a float field and must paginate on that, an
example CursorPagination subclass that uses decimals to limit precision is available here (https://gist.github.com/keturn/8bc88525a183fd41c73ffb729b8865be#file-fpcursorpagination-py)
.)
The field should have a database index.

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly
`CursorPagination`
ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
Supports usage with very large datasets. With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable. Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail. You'll need to think about what ordering you want the scheme to be applied against. The default is to order by
`"-created"`
. This assumes that
there must be a 'created' timestamp field
on the model instances, and will present a "timeline" style paginated view, with the most recently added items first.

Using an ordering field that does not satisfy these constraints will generally still work, but you'll be losing some of the benefits of cursor pagination.

For more technical details on the implementation we use for cursor pagination, the
"Building cursors for the Disqus API" (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
blog post gives a good overview of the basic approach.

#### Setup¶ {#setup_2}

To enable the
`CursorPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration, modifying the
`PAGE_SIZE`
as desired:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.CursorPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`


On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`CursorPagination`
on a per-view basis.

#### Configuration¶ {#configuration_2}

The
`CursorPagination`
class includes a number of attributes that may be overridden to modify the pagination style.

To set these attributes you should override the
`CursorPagination`
class, and then enable your custom pagination class as above.

`page_size`
= A numeric value indicating the page size. If set, this overrides the
`PAGE_SIZE`
setting. Defaults to the same value as the
`PAGE_SIZE`
settings key.
`cursor_query_param`
= A string value indicating the name of the "cursor" query parameter. Defaults to
`'cursor'`
.
`ordering`
= This should be a string, or list of strings, indicating the field against which the cursor based pagination will be applied. For example:
`ordering = 'slug'`
. Defaults to
`-created`
. This value may also be overridden by using
`OrderingFilter`
on the view.
`template`
= The name of a template to use when rendering pagination controls in the browsable API. May be overridden to modify the rendering style, or set to
`None`
to disable HTML pagination controls completely. Defaults to
`"rest_framework/pagination/previous_and_next.html"`
.

You can modify the ordering by overriding the
`'ordering'`
attribute on the pagination class, or by using the
`OrderingFilter`
filter class together with
`CursorPagination`

`OrderingFilter`
you should strongly consider restricting the fields that the user may order by.

#### New pagination schemes.¶ {#new-pagination-schemes}

Until now, there has only been a single built-in pagination style in REST framework. We now have page, limit/offset and cursor based schemes included by default.

The cursor based pagination scheme is particularly smart, and is a better approach for clients iterating through large or frequently changing result sets. The scheme supports paging against non-unique indexes, by using both cursor and limit/offset information. It also allows for both forward and reverse cursor pagination. Much credit goes to David Cramer for
this blog post (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
on the subject.

user_input: We run three application servers behind a load balancer and a client on a 100/day allowance managed roughly 300 before anything stopped it — almost exactly three times what it should be. Each server has its own local in-process cache. I think I know what's happening, but I need to understand where the counting actually lives: what does a throttle count against, and how do I move that somewhere all three servers can see?
reference: Your read is right, and the two halves are one story. Throttles are counters held in the cache, keyed per client — for a scoped throttle the key is formed by concatenating the request's scope with the unique user id, or with the IP address for unauthenticated clients. With a local per-process cache each server keeps its own independent counter under that key, so each one grants the full allowance and you get roughly N× your configured rate across N servers. Moving the counters to a backend all three share fixes it. Throttles use the 'default' cache unless told otherwise, and the documented way to point them elsewhere is to subclass the throttle and set its `cache` attribute — `class CustomAnonRateThrottle(AnonRateThrottle): cache = caches['alternate']` — then remember to register that subclass in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES or the view's throttle_classes, since defining it alone changes nothing.
reference_contexts: If you need to use a cache other than 'default', you can do so by creating a custom throttle class and setting the cache attribute.
from django.core.cache import caches class CustomAnonRateThrottle(AnonRateThrottle): cache = caches['alternate']
You'll need to remember to also set your custom throttle class in the 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES' settings key, or using the throttle_classes view attribute.
The unique throttle key will then be formed by concatenating the "scope" of the request with the unique user id or IP address.
llm_response:
A throttle counts against a unique key generated by the throttle class (for example, the IP address of the incoming request for `AnonRateThrottle`). Because you are using the default `LocMemCache` backend, each of your three servers maintains its own local, in-process cache. Consequently, each server is tracking the throttle count independently, which explains why the client is allowed three times the intended limit.

To move the counting to a location all three servers can see, you must configure a shared cache backend in your Django settings (such as Redis or Memcached) instead of using the default `LocMemCache`. 

Once you have configured a shared cache in your Django `CACHES` setting, REST framework will use it automatically because the throttle classes use Django's cache backend. If you need to use a specific cache other than the one defined as `'default'`, you can create a custom throttle class and set the `cache` attribute:

```python
from django.core.cache import caches
from rest_framework.throttling import AnonRateThrottle

class CustomAnonRateThrottle(AnonRateThrottle):
    cache = caches['alternate']
```

After creating a custom class, you must register it in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings using the `'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES'` key or the `throttle_classes` view attribute.

## A note on concurrency¶ {#a-note-on-concurrency}

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

## A note on concurrency¶ {#a-note-on-concurrency}

The built-in throttle implementations are open to
race conditions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_condition#Data_race)
, so under high concurrency they may allow a few extra requests through.

If your project relies on guaranteeing the number of requests during concurrent requests, you will need to implement your own throttle class. See
issue #5181 (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/issues/5181)
for more details.

# Throttling¶ {#throttling}

HTTP/1.1 420 Enhance Your Calm

Throttling is similar to
permissions (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
, in that it determines if a request should be authorized.  Throttles indicate a temporary state, and are used to control the rate of requests that clients can make to an API.

As with permissions, multiple throttles may be used.  Your API might have a restrictive throttle for unauthenticated requests, and a less restrictive throttle for authenticated requests.

Another scenario where you might want to use multiple throttles would be if you need to impose different constraints on different parts of the API, due to some services being particularly resource-intensive.

The application-level throttling provided by REST framework is intended for implementing policies such as different business tiers and basic protections against service over-use.

## How throttling is determined¶ {#how-throttling-is-determined}

As with permissions and authentication, throttling in REST framework is always defined as a list of classes.

Before running the main body of the view each throttle in the list is checked.
If any throttle check fails an
`exceptions.Throttled`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

## Setting the throttling policy¶ {#setting-the-throttling-policy}

The default throttling policy may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
settings.  For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle','rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle'],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'anon':'100/day','user':'1000/day'}}`

`X-Forwarded-For`
header, once any application proxy IP addresses have first been excluded.  If set to zero, then the
`REMOTE_ADDR`
value will always be used as the identifying IP address.

It is important to understand that if you configure the
`NUM_PROXIES`

NAT'd (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_address_translation)
gateway will be treated as a single client.

Further context on how the
`X-Forwarded-For`
header works, and identifying a remote client IP can be
found here (http://oxpedia.org/wiki/index.php?title=AppSuite:Grizzly#Multiple_Proxies_in_front_of_the_cluster)

user_input: I hung a custom action off one of our viewsets. It routes fine and I can call it, but two things aren't behaving: the object-level permission I attached to it never seems to be consulted, and after I changed the URL segment to be hyphenated instead of underscored, the link our serializer builds to it started raising NoReverseMatch. How does an action of this kind get its URL and its permissions — are these the same knob or two?
reference: Two knobs, and the URL one is itself two values. The router picks up methods decorated with @action and generates routes for them, with `detail=True` or `detail=False` deciding whether the pattern carries a pk. By default the URL pattern comes from the method name and the URL *name* is the viewset's basename joined to the hyphenated method name — and `url_path` and `url_name` change those two independently. Changing only url_path leaves the reverse name as it was, so a serializer reversing the name you assumed gets NoReverseMatch; set both, or reverse the name that's actually registered. Permissions are separate: @action accepts `permission_classes`, e.g. @action(detail=True, methods=['post'], permission_classes=[IsAdminOrIsSelf]). Two things stop those from firing. Object-level checks only run when the object is fetched through get_object(), so an action that queries the model directly never triggers them — call self.check_object_permissions() yourself if you do. And do not wire an @action method up with .as_view(): that bypasses router setup and may ignore action settings including permission_classes, which is the usual cause of a permission that appears to be attached but never runs.
reference_contexts: If you have ad-hoc methods that should be routable, you can mark them as such with the @action decorator. Like regular actions, extra actions may be intended for either a single object, or an entire collection. To indicate this, set the detail argument to True or False. The router will configure its URL patterns accordingly.

By default, the URL pattern is based on the method name, and the URL name is the combination of the ViewSet.basename and the hyphenated method name. If you don't want to use the defaults for either of these values, you can instead provide the url_path and url_name arguments to the @action decorator.
@action(detail=True, methods=['post'], permission_classes=[IsAdminOrIsSelf]) def set_password(self, request, pk=None): ...
Do not use .as_view() with @action methods. It bypasses router setup and may ignore action settings like permission_classes. Use DefaultRouter for actions.

These are two separate knobs.

### URL Generation and `NoReverseMatch`
The URL pattern and the URL name are controlled by the `url_path` and `url_name` arguments in the `@action` decorator. 
*   **URL Path:** By default, the URL segment is based on the method name. If you change the segment manually, you must use the `url_path` argument to define it.
*   **URL Name:** By default, the URL name is the combination of the `ViewSet.basename` and the hyphenated method name. If you change the method name or the URL segment, the default URL name may no longer match what your serializer expects. 

To fix the `NoReverseMatch` error, you must ensure the `url_name` argument in your `@action` decorator matches the name your serializer is attempting to reverse. You can verify the correct name by checking the `url_name` attribute set on the decorated method. When reversing these URLs in code, use the `.reverse_action()` method, which is a convenience wrapper that automatically handles the `basename` and `request` object:
`self.reverse_action(self.your_action_name.url_name, args=[pk])`

### Permissions
Permissions are controlled by the `permission_classes` argument within the `@action` decorator. This is a separate knob from the URL configuration. If your object-level permissions are not being consulted, ensure that the `permission_classes` list is correctly passed to the `@action` decorator, as shown here:

```python
@action(methods=['post'], detail=True, permission_classes=[IsAdminOrIsSelf])
def your_action(self, request, pk=None):
    ...
```

The `ViewSet` class inherits from `APIView` and uses standard attributes like `permission_classes` to control API policy. If you are not using a router, you must provide the `basename` argument to the `.as_view()` method for URL reversing to function correctly.

The `ModelSerializer` does not support writable nested fields by default. Because you have not defined an explicit `.create()` method in your `UserSerializer`, the nested `profile` data is being ignored during the save process, which is why the user is created but the profile is not.

## CSRF protection¶ {#csrf-protection}

Cross Site Request Forgery (https://www.owasp.org/index.php/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_(CSRF))
protection is a mechanism of guarding against a particular type of attack, which can occur when a user has not logged out of a web site, and continues to have a valid session.   In this circumstance a malicious site may be able to perform actions against the target site, within the context of the logged-in session.

Warning
Always use Django's standard login view when creating login pages. This will ensure your login views are properly protected.

CSRF validation in REST framework works slightly differently from standard Django due to the need to support both session and non-session based authentication to the same views. This means that only authenticated requests require CSRF tokens, and anonymous requests may be sent without CSRF tokens. This behavior is not suitable for login views, which should always have CSRF validation applied.

## How authentication is determined¶ {#how-authentication-is-determined}

The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
using the return value of the first class that successfully authenticates.

If no class authenticates,

The permission works on the detail endpoint because generic views check object-level permissions for views that retrieve a single model instance. However, for performance reasons, generic views do not automatically apply object-level permissions to each instance in a queryset when returning a list of objects. Consequently, permission checks for list actions are applied to the entire object type rather than individual instances.

To scope a list response, you must filter the queryset separately. The recommended approach is to override the `get_queryset()` method in your view to restrict the results based on the currently authenticated user.

    for the currently authenticated user.
    """
    user = self.request.user
    return Purchase.objects.filter(owner=user)

## Overview of access restriction methods¶ {#overview-of-access-restriction-methods}

REST framework offers three different methods to customize access restrictions on a case-by-case basis. These apply in different scenarios and have different effects and limitations.

`queryset`
/
`get_queryset()`
: Limits the general visibility of existing objects from the database. The queryset limits which objects will be listed and which objects can be modified or deleted. The
`get_queryset()`
method can apply different querysets based on the current action.
`permission_classes`
/
`get_permissions()`
: General permission checks based on the current action, request and targeted object. Object level permissions can only be applied to retrieve, modify and deletion actions. Permission checks for list and create will be applied to the entire object type. (In case of list: subject to restrictions in the queryset.)
`serializer_class`
/
`get_serializer()`
: Instance level restrictions that apply to all objects on input and output. The serializer may have access to the request context. The
`get_serializer()`
method can apply different serializers based on the current action.

Overriding this method allows you to customize the queryset returned by the view in a number of different ways.

To accept raw file uploads from native clients, you must use the `FileUploadParser`. The 415 error occurs because your view is currently using the default parsers, which do not support raw binary streams.

### Implementation Steps

1.  **Update your view**: Add `parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]` to your `UploadView`. Because `FileUploadParser` has a media type of `*/*`, it should generally be the only parser set on the view.
2.  **Handle the filename**: Since you are already passing `filename` as a URL keyword argument, `FileUploadParser` will automatically use that value as the filename.

**Updated `views.py`:**
```python
from rest_framework.parsers import FileUploadParser
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response

class UploadView(APIView):
    parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]

    def put(self, request, filename):
        file_obj = request.data['file']
        # save(file_obj, filename)
        return Response(status=204)
```

### Why this works
*   **Parser Selection**: When you access `request.data`, the framework examines the `Content-Type` header. By setting `parser_classes`, you ensure the request is handled by the `FileUploadParser` instead of raising an `UnsupportedMediaType` exception (415).
*   **Filename**: The documentation specifies that if the view is called with a `filename` URL keyword argument, that argument is used as the filename.
*   **Streaming**: `FileUploadParser` is designed for native clients uploading files as raw data requests. It respects Django's `FILE_UPLOAD_HANDLERS` setting, allowing you to handle large files without buffering the entire request into memory.

# Parsers¶ {#parsers}

Machine interacting web services tend to use more
structured formats for sending data than form-encoded, since they're
sending more complex data than simple forms
— Malcom Tredinnick,
Django developers group (https://groups.google.com/d/topic/django-developers/dxI4qVzrBY4/discussion)

REST framework includes a number of built-in Parser classes, that allow you to accept requests with various media types.  There is also support for defining your own custom parsers, which gives you the flexibility to design the media types that your API accepts.

## How the parser is determined¶ {#how-the-parser-is-determined}

The set of valid parsers for a view is always defined as a list of classes.  When
`request.data`
is accessed, REST framework will examine the
`Content-Type`
header on the incoming request, and determine which parser to use to parse the request content.

You won't typically need to access this property.

Note
If a client sends malformed content, then accessing
`request.data`
may raise a
`ParseError`
.  By default REST framework's
`APIView`
class or
`@api_view`
decorator will catch the error and return a
`400 Bad Request`
response.
If a client sends a request with a content-type that cannot be parsed then a
`UnsupportedMediaType`
exception will be raised, which by default will be caught and return a
`415 Unsupported Media Type`
response.

The request exposes some properties that allow you to determine the result of the content negotiation stage. This allows you to implement behavior such as selecting a different serialization schemes for different media types.

According to the documentation, the type of response returned when authentication fails is determined by the highest priority (first) authentication class set on the view [1, 2]. 

*   **`SessionAuthentication`** is documented to result in an `HTTP 403 Forbidden` response for unauthenticated requests [5].
*   **`BasicAuthentication`** is documented to result in an `HTTP 401 Unauthorized` response with a `WWW-Authenticate` header [4].

Because `SessionAuthentication` appears first in your `authentication_classes` list, it determines the response type, causing the 403.

To fix this, you should reorder your `authentication_classes` so that an authentication scheme that uses `WWW-Authenticate` headers (such as `BasicAuthentication`) is listed first:

```python
class ReportView(APIView):
    authentication_classes = [BasicAuthentication, SessionAuthentication]
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]
```

By placing `BasicAuthentication` first, the system will use it to determine the response type, resulting in a 401 when the request is unauthenticated [1, 2].

The `OrderingFilter` defaults to allowing ordering on any readable fields on the serializer if an `ordering_fields` attribute is not specified on the view. Because you have not defined `ordering_fields`, the filter is permitting ordering against model fields that are accessible to the queryset.

To constrain the fields that can be ordered against, you must explicitly set the `ordering_fields` attribute on your view. This is the recommended approach to prevent unexpected data leakage.

Update your view as follows:

```python
class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.OrderingFilter]
    ordering_fields = ['username'] # Add only the fields you wish to expose
```

By defining this list, you restrict the API to only allow ordering against the specified fields.

By overriding the `get_object()` method, you bypassed the automatic execution of object-level permissions that REST framework's generic views perform when calling that method. Because you did not explicitly call `self.check_object_permissions(self.request, obj)` after retrieving the object, the `IsOwnerOrReadOnly` permission class is not being applied to your retrieved instance, allowing unauthorized users to perform PUT or DELETE actions.

To fix this, you must add the check to your `get_object` method:

```python
def get_object(self):
    obj = get_object_or_404(
        Thing, account=self.kwargs['account'], slug=self.kwargs['slug']
    )
    self.check_object_permissions(self.request, obj)
    return obj
```

This call will trigger the `has_object_permission()` method in your `IsOwnerOrReadOnly` class and raise a `PermissionDenied` exception if the user is not the owner.

### ScopedRateThrottle¶ {#scopedratethrottle}

The
`ScopedRateThrottle`
class can be used to restrict access to specific parts of the API.  This throttle will only be applied if the view that is being accessed includes a
`.throttle_scope`
property.  The unique throttle key will then be formed by concatenating the "scope" of the request with the unique user id or IP address.

The allowed request rate is determined by the
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
setting using a key from the request "scope".

For example, given the following views...


`classContactListView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classContactDetailView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classUploadView(APIView):throttle_scope='uploads'...`


...and the following settings.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`

...and the following settings.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`


User requests to either
`ContactListView`
or
`ContactDetailView`
would be restricted to a total of 1000 requests per-day.  User requests to
`UploadView`
would be restricted to 20 requests per day.

## Custom throttles¶ {#custom-throttles}

To create a custom throttle, override
`BaseThrottle`
and implement
`.allow_request(self, request, view)`
.  The method should return
`True`
if the request should be allowed, and
`False`
otherwise.

Optionally you may also override the
`.wait()`
method.  If implemented,
`.wait()`
should return a recommended number of seconds to wait before attempting the next request, or
`None`
.  The
`.wait()`
method will only be called if
`.allow_request()`
has previously returned
`False`
.

# Throttling¶ {#throttling}

HTTP/1.1 420 Enhance Your Calm
Twitter API rate limiting response (https://developer.twitter.com/en/docs/basics/rate-limiting)

Throttling is similar to
permissions (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
, in that it determines if a request should be authorized.  Throttles indicate a temporary state, and are used to control the rate of requests that clients can make to an API.

As with permissions, multiple throttles may be used.  Your API might have a restrictive throttle for unauthenticated requests, and a less restrictive throttle for authenticated requests.

Another scenario where you might want to use multiple throttles would be if you need to impose different constraints on different parts of the API, due to some services being particularly resource-intensive.

## A note on concurrency¶ {#a-note-on-concurrency}

The built-in throttle implementations are open to
race conditions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_condition#Data_race)
, so under high concurrency they may allow a few extra requests through.

If your project relies on guaranteeing the number of requests during concurrent requests, you will need to implement your own throttle class. See
issue #5181 (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/issues/5181)
for more details.

## API Reference¶ {#api-reference}

### AnonRateThrottle¶ {#anonratethrottle}

The
`AnonRateThrottle`
will only ever throttle unauthenticated users.  The IP address of the incoming request is used to generate a unique key to throttle against.

The allowed request rate is determined from one of the following (in order of preference).

The
`rate`
property on the class, which may be provided by overriding
`AnonRateThrottle`
and setting the property.
The
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES['anon']`
setting.

The
`rate`
property on the class, which may be provided by overriding
`AnonRateThrottle`
and setting the property.
The
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES['anon']`
setting.

`AnonRateThrottle`
is suitable if you want to restrict the rate of requests from unknown sources.

### UserRateThrottle¶ {#userratethrottle}

The
`UserRateThrottle`
will throttle users to a given rate of requests across the API.  The user id is used to generate a unique key to throttle against.  Unauthenticated requests will fall back to using the IP address of the incoming request to generate a unique key to throttle against.

The allowed request rate is determined from one of the following (in order of preference).

The
`rate`
property on the class, which may be provided by overriding
`UserRateThrottle`
and setting the property.
The
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES['user']`
setting.

The
`rate`
property on the class, which may be provided by overriding
`UserRateThrottle`
and setting the property.
The
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES['user']`
setting.

An API may have multiple
`UserRateThrottles`
in place at the same time.  To do so, override
`UserRateThrottle`
and set a unique "scope" for each class.

For example, multiple user throttle rates could be implemented by using the following classes...


`classBurstRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle):scope='burst'classSustainedRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle):scope='sustained'`


...and the following settings.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['example.throttles.BurstRateThrottle','example.throttles.SustainedRateThrottle'],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'burst':'60/min','sustained':'1000/day'}}`


`UserRateThrottle`
is suitable if you want simple global rate restrictions per-user.

### ScopedRateThrottle¶ {#scopedratethrottle}

The application-level throttling provided by REST framework is intended for implementing policies such as different business tiers and basic protections against service over-use.

## How throttling is determined¶ {#how-throttling-is-determined}

As with permissions and authentication, throttling in REST framework is always defined as a list of classes.

Before running the main body of the view each throttle in the list is checked.
If any throttle check fails an
`exceptions.Throttled`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

## Setting the throttling policy¶ {#setting-the-throttling-policy}

The default throttling policy may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
settings.  For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle','rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle'],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'anon':'100/day','user':'1000/day'}}`

REST framework provides two wrappers you can use to write API views.

The
`@api_view`
decorator for working with function based views.
The

reference: A read_only field is excluded from writable fields, so it won't use a default for input — that's why the default is ignored. If you want the value auto-set and hidden from input, use HiddenField with a default (e.g. a callable), which lands in validated_data but isn't in the output.

llm_response:
The default is being skipped because `read_only=True` fields are excluded from writable fields, and as of version 3.8.0, they are always excluded from using a `default` argument.

To achieve a server-set timestamp that the client cannot set or spoof and that is not required in the request body, you should use `serializers.HiddenField`. This field type does not accept user input and always returns its default value to the `validated_data`.

You should implement it as follows:

```python
created = serializers.HiddenField(default=timezone.now)
```

If you specifically require the timestamp to be set only during create operations (and omitted during updates), you can use `CreateOnlyDefault`:

```python
created = serializers.HiddenField(default=serializers.CreateOnlyDefault(timezone.now))
```

The `SerializerMethodField` defaults to looking for a method named `get_<field_name>` on the serializer class [1, 2, 3]. Because your field is named `days_since_joined`, the serializer is attempting to call a method named `get_days_since_joined`.

Since your method is named `compute_days`, the serializer does not find the expected method, resulting in the `null` value.

To fix this, you have two options:

1.  **Rename your method** to `get_days_since_joined(self, obj)` to match the default naming convention [1, 3].
2.  **Specify the method name** in the field definition:
    `days_since_joined = serializers.SerializerMethodField(method_name='compute_days')` [1, 2]

llm_response:
To achieve the requirement where the server fills the field during creation but leaves it untouched during updates, you should use `serializers.CreateOnlyDefault`.

You can implement this in your `PostSerializer` as follows:

```python
from django.utils import timezone

class PostSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    created_at = serializers.DateTimeField(default=serializers.CreateOnlyDefault(timezone.now))

    class Meta:
        model = Post
        fields = ['id', 'body', 'created_at']
```

**Why this works:**
*   **`CreateOnlyDefault`**: This default class is specifically designed to set a default value or callable only during create operations. During updates, the field is omitted, ensuring the existing value is not overwritten by the default.
*   **Handling PUT/Update**: Because the field is omitted during updates when no input is provided, the existing stored value will survive untouched.

Getting sporadic 500s from a line that shouldn't be able to fail. It's roughly 1 in 50 requests and I cannot reproduce it locally.

# views.py
if request.user.is_authenticated:   # <- traceback points here
    ...

# authentication.py

    def authenticate(self, request):
        username = request.META['HTTP_X_USERNAME']
        user = User.objects.get(username=username)
        return (user, None)

The exception is an AttributeError, but the object it's complaining about has nothing to do with anything on that line, and the traceback goes through a property in DRF's request module rather than my code. My first instinct was that DRF has a bug, since I'm not calling my authenticator there at all. What's the chain here?
reference: When your authenticator is invoked via request.user/.auth, an AttributeError it raises is re-raised as a WrappedAttributeError so it isn't silently swallowed by the property access. It signals a real error in your authenticator (here, KeyError/AttributeError on the missing header) that you need to fix or handle.
reference_contexts: Note When your custom authenticator is invoked by the request object's .user or .auth properties, you may see an AttributeError re-raised as a WrappedAttributeError .
These errors should be fixed or otherwise handled by your authenticator.
llm_response:
The chain of events is as follows:

1.  **Triggering Authentication:** When you access `request.user` in your view, DRF invokes your authentication classes to determine the user.
2.  **The `AttributeError`:** Your `HeaderAuthentication` class attempts to access `request.META['HTTP_X_USERNAME']`. If a request arrives without this header, Python raises a standard `AttributeError` (or `KeyError`) because the key is missing.
3.  **The `WrappedAttributeError`:** Because this error occurs during the property access of `.user`, DRF catches the `AttributeError` and re-raises it as a `WrappedAttributeError`. This is done to prevent Python from incorrectly assuming the `request` object lacks a `.user` property entirely.
4.  **The Result:** The traceback points to the property access in DRF because it is re-raising the exception that originated in your authenticator.

**How to fix it:**
Your authenticator must be updated to handle missing headers or missing users safely. Instead of accessing `request.META` directly, you should check for the existence of the header and return `None` if it is missing, which allows other authentication schemes to be checked.

Follow the pattern shown in the documentation [7]:

```python
def authenticate(self, request):
    username = request.META.get('HTTP_X_USERNAME')
    if not username:
        return None
    try:
        user = User.objects.get(username=username)
    except User.DoesNotExist:
        raise exceptions.AuthenticationFailed('No such user')
    return (user, None)
```

By using `.get()` and checking for the existence of the username, you prevent the `AttributeError` from being raised in the first place.

and

settings.

This is not a bug. All Django REST framework (DRF) views are opted-out of `LoginRequiredMiddleware` because the middleware's redirect behavior is unsuitable for APIs, which should return a 401 status code instead.

To enforce a blanket requirement that API requests must be logged in, you must configure the global DRF settings in your `settings.py` file. Specifically, you should set `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` to `IsAuthenticated`.

Add the following to your `settings.py`:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',
    ],
}
```

This ensures that all API views require authentication by default. If you need to specify authentication schemes globally as well, you can also define `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` within the same `REST_FRAMEWORK` dictionary.

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)

This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied. `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

llm_response:
Calling the view directly with `APIRequestFactory` behaves differently because, unlike Django's standard `RequestFactory`, REST framework performs CSRF validation inside the view. When testing views directly, middleware is not run, so the CSRF validation that would normally be handled by middleware in a browser request is instead triggered within the view.

The recommended way to write these tests is to use the `APIClient` class instead of `APIRequestFactory`. `APIClient` extends Django's standard `Client` class and supports the same request interface (e.g., `.post()`, `.put()`), but it handles the request lifecycle more similarly to how the browser interacts with the API.

If you must continue using `APIRequestFactory` or need to explicitly enable CSRF validation, you can do so by setting the `enforce_csrf_checks` flag to `True` when instantiating the factory:

```python
factory = APIRequestFactory(enforce_csrf_checks=True)
```

Additionally, because you are using `SessionAuthentication`, note that `APIRequestFactory` returns a standard Django `HttpRequest` rather than a REST framework `Request` object. If you need to authenticate the request, you should use the `force_authenticate()` helper:

```python
from rest_framework.test import force_authenticate

request = factory.post('/notes/', {'title': 'x'}, format='json')
force_authenticate(request, user=user)

```

This means that setting attributes directly on the request object may not always have the effect you expect.  For example, setting
`.token`
directly will have no effect, and setting
`.user`
directly will only work if session authentication is being used.

For example, using
`APIRequestFactory`
, you can make a form PUT request like so:


`factory=APIRequestFactory()request=factory.put('/notes/547/',{'title':'remember to email dave'})`


Using Django's
`RequestFactory`
, you'd need to explicitly encode the data yourself:


`fromdjango.test.clientimportencode_multipart,RequestFactoryfactory=RequestFactory()data={'title':'remember to email dave'}content=encode_multipart('BoUnDaRyStRiNg',data)content_type='multipart/form-data; boundary=BoUnDaRyStRiNg'request=factory.put('/notes/547/',content,content_type=content_type)`


### Forcing authentication¶ {#forcing-authentication}

When testing views directly using a request factory, it's often convenient to be able to directly authenticate the request, rather than having to construct the correct authentication credentials.

To forcibly authenticate a request, use the
`force_authenticate()`
method.

#### .force_authenticate(user=None, token=None)¶ {#force_authenticateusernone-tokennone}

Sometimes you may want to bypass authentication entirely and force all requests by the test client to be automatically treated as authenticated.

This can be a useful shortcut if you're testing the API but don't want to have to construct valid authentication credentials in order to make test requests.


`user=User.objects.get(username='lauren')client=APIClient()client.force_authenticate(user=user)`


To unauthenticate subsequent requests, call
`force_authenticate`
setting the user and/or token to
`None`
.


`client.force_authenticate(user=None)`


### CSRF validation¶ {#csrf-validation}

By default CSRF validation is not applied when using
`APIClient`
.  If you need to explicitly enable CSRF validation, you can do so by setting the
`enforce_csrf_checks`
flag when instantiating the client.


`client=APIClient(enforce_csrf_checks=True)`
